newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel Netanyahu tries to ease tensions with Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Israel Netanyahu tries to ease tensions with Arafat.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent an envoy to Yasser Arafat and later spoke by phone with the Palestinian president in a bid to calm tensions over government benefits for Jewish settlers in the West Bank.
Asked what he relayed to Arafat in the telephone call, Netanyahu told Israel's Itim news agency: "A message of peace."

The meeting in Gaza between Arafat and Netanyahu adviser Yitzhak Molcho was the first such high-level contact in weeks between Israel and the PLO, a spokesman for Arafat said. No details were immediately available about the night-time meeting.

Earlier, Netanyahu launched a media offensive in a series of interviews with Israeli radio and television stations to defend his cabinet's decision on Friday to grant benefits, such a tax breaks, to West Bank settlers.

The Palestinian Information Ministry has called the Israeli move a declaration of war. Some 130,000 Jews live amidst two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, areas captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

Netanyahu accused Palestinians of plotting violence even before he reinstated the financial incentives, cancelled by the Labour-led government he defeated in elections last May, for Jews to settle in West Bank.

"There is clear information that the Palestinian side, senior elements on the Palestinian side, have been planning, without connection to the government decision, for weeks, planning another wave of violence," he told Israel Radio.

Netanyahu said he told U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk of his government's decision before it was formally taken. Washington called the aid to settlers, given after guerrillas killed a settler and her son last week, "troubling".
Anticipating Netanyahu's attack, Arafat was quoted by an Israeli daily saying Jewish settlement was a time bomb -- and Netanyahu had turned to "cheap propoganda" because he knew it.

Arafat told reporters in Gaza on Sunday: "As for the statements of the Israeli prime minister today that we are preparing to wage war on them, this is untrue and aims at diverting attention from what he is preparing to do against us ...This government does not want peace."
Netanyahu hinted there would come a time for new Jewish settlements on occupied land. Since taking office, he has approved plans to build thousands of homes in existing settlements.
"It is correct that we will decide at our own timing, in our own way, on expanding on new territories," Netanyahu told the radio.

He also criticised Israeli opposition parties, who have warned the policies he has pursued since taking office in June will destroy the Arab-Israeli peace process launched by the previous Labour government in 1991.
Netanyahu said the Israeli opposition should instead be attacking "the clear attempt by the Palestinian Authority to ignite the area."
He dismissed as inaccurate reports that security chiefs have warned him settlement expansion would cause violence.

His opening of an entrance to a tunnel near Moslem sites in Arab East Jerusalem in September spurred clashes in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed. Local media said security chiefs had warned it would spark clashes.
